name: PicoClaw
vibe_summary: An ultra-lightweight Go rewrite of the personal AI assistant concept, built from scratch by Sipeed to run on $10 hardware with under 10MB of RAM. It targets extreme portability across x86, ARM, MIPS, RISC-V, and LoongArch with millisecond boot times.
best_for: Running an AI assistant on cheap SBCs or embedded boards
Users who want minimal RAM footprint and instant startup
Self-hosters on RISC-V, MIPS, or other exotic architectures
avoid_if: You need a rich plugin ecosystem or mature integrations
You want OS-level sandboxing for tool execution
You rely on niche chat channels that may lag upstream API changes
openclaw_advantages: Runs in under 10MB RAM versus OpenClaw's much heavier footprint
Single Go binary deployable across many CPU architectures
Smaller codebase is easier to audit and self-modify
openclaw_disadvantages: Far fewer integrations, skills, and UI features than OpenClaw
No true OS-level sandboxing for agent tool execution
Smaller community and thinner documentation depth
Some chat-channel integrations lag upstream API changes

overview_markdown:
PicoClaw is an independent open-source personal AI assistant written entirely in Go by Sipeed, inspired by NanoBot but rebuilt from scratch through a self-bootstrapping process where the AI agent itself drove the architecture migration. Its headline claim is extreme efficiency: it runs on $10 hardware with under 10MB of RAM and millisecond boot times, roughly 99% less memory than OpenClaw, and ships as a single binary supporting x86_64, ARM64, MIPS, RISC-V, and LoongArch.

Architecturally, PicoClaw focuses on a lean core with configurable model provider fallback chains, multi-provider support (Anthropic, Bedrock, OpenAI-compatible), and a tool system with guardrails — for example, recent work steers write_file away from destructive overwrites toward append/edit tools when available. Recent commits show active maintenance including security-driven dependency updates (govulncheck fixes) and provider bug fixes for tool-call history handling.

Compared to OpenClaw, PicoClaw trades feature breadth for footprint: it lacks the full Control UI, extensive skills library, and mature channel integrations, but it is the clear choice for constrained edge devices and users who want an auditable, minimal Go codebase. It is best understood as an edge-first alternative rather than a feature-parity clone.
